Before you start

Each slide carries its own point, so you can talk with the room instead of reading notes. Keep it light and curious. Let students between friend groups stay private, and never treat having few friends as a failing. If a student says nothing feels good anymore, walk them to a counselor that day.

Every student in the room

Families and cultures picture a good life differently (excitement or calm, achievement or family, faith or freedom), and some students are between friend groups or lonely right now; honor every version and never treat having few friends as a failing.

Slides and notes

Tap any slide to present from there.

Slide 1 · Notes

Keep it light for ten seconds, then go straight to the next slide.

Slide 2 · Notes

A minute of silence, then a few volunteers. Some will say it still feels great; say that’s fine. Ask: why does the thing we wanted so much fade so fast?

Slide 3 · Notes

Dopamine is about anticipation more than pleasure. Pleasure comes from a few small spots; wanting runs through a much larger network. Feeds and likes run on unpredictable rewards, exactly what wanting responds to. Cards: rate one thing from yesterday, want and like, 1 to 10.

Slide 4 · Notes

Impact bias: you picture the moment you find out, not an ordinary Tuesday three months later with laundry and a lab report. We adapt, but the baseline can shift, and what you do with your time can move it. Money helps most people; say clearly it matters, especially when there isn’t enough.

Slide 5 · Notes

Hands up for each. Next slide shows the answer. The Harvard study has run more than 85 years.

Slide 6 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 7 · Notes

Two minutes. Keep it light. Students between friend groups can answer about anything.

Slide 8 · Notes

Take a few. Count how many include another person.

Slide 9 · Notes

The liking gap says she comes across better than she thinks.

Slide 10 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 11 · Notes

Friendship takes hours, and nine months is plenty for a few.

Slide 12 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 13 · Notes

No single right answer. Some families need the paid job, and that’s a real reason. Ask which bet they’d make.

Slide 14 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 15 · Notes

Hands up for each. Next slide shows the answer. People also like us more than we think: the liking gap.

Slide 16 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 17 · Notes

Do things with people, not just near them. Cultures differ in the good feeling people aim for, excitement or calm. Ask students to think privately about what their family hopes their life will feel like.

Slide 18 · Notes

Honor every version. Some students are between friend groups or lonely right now; never treat that as a failing.

Slide 19 · Notes

Two minutes in pairs. Nobody speaks for a group, and no personal stories.

Slide 20 · Notes

Take a few. Listen for strengths as well as costs.

Slide 21 · Notes

Students write it on a card and keep it; sending is up to them. The other person is likely more glad than they’d guess. Share the take-home link.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can explain the difference between wanting and liking, why we overestimate how happy a goal will make us, and what the research says pays off most: time with people. They leave with one small bet to try this week. A good life looks different across families and cultures, and the lesson leaves room for that.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • The take-home link to share after the talk

Flow

  1. 5 minThink back
  2. 8 minOne wants, one enjoys
  3. 5 minA bad fortune teller
  4. 3 minThe health at 80 guess
  5. 5 minSmall good things: turn and talk, share out
  6. 10 minWhich bet pays off? Sofia, Nick, Lily
  7. 4 minThe commuters, and what lasts
  8. 5 minEvery student, close: one small bet

Short on time (20-minute advisory)

Think back, want and like, the health at 80 guess, one bet, and one text to send.

Before you teach
Some students are lonely right now.

The "one solid person" check can sting for a student who's between friend groups, especially after a move. Keep it private, and say out loud that it's common and not a verdict on anyone.

Don't knock ambition.

Students who are working hard for college, a team or a job should hear that their goals are worth chasing. The lesson is about not putting all of life on hold until then.

Be fair about money.

Some students' families are under real money pressure. Say plainly that money matters, especially when there isn't enough. It's one ingredient, not the whole recipe.

Watch for low mood.

If a student says nothing feels good anymore, even things they used to love, or that they feel hopeless, take it seriously and walk them to a counselor that day. 988 is there any time.

Keep the phone piece light.

The point is "did I like that, or just want more of it?" Not a lecture about screens.

Make the text real but optional.

Inviting students to send one text to someone they miss works well. Make sure nobody has to show what they wrote.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Different pictures of a good life.

Jeanne Tsai's research finds cultures differ in the good feeling people aim for: some lean toward excitement, others toward calm and contentment. Neither is right. Invite students to ask what their family hopes their life will feel like.

Family duty.

For some students, caring for siblings, working in a family business or honoring parents' sacrifices is part of what makes life meaningful. Count it as "caring about something beyond you," not as a barrier to happiness.

Money and work.

Lily's choice (paid camp job or unpaid internship) is easier for some families than others. Some students don't have the option to work unpaid. Treat the paid job as just as legitimate.

Faith.

For many students, faith is a central source of meaning and community. Include it by name when talking about what lasts.

New students and movers.

Nick's card fits students who moved, immigrated or changed schools. The 50, 90 and 200 hours for friendship can be reassuring: it takes time for everyone.

Neurodivergent and shy students.

Talking to strangers costs more for some students. Offer smaller versions: one text, one weekly activity, one person at lunch.

What the research says

Wanting runs through a large dopamine network, while the feeling of enjoyment comes from a few small hotspots, such as the ventral pallidum.

Berridge and Kringelbach, Neuron, 2015

People overestimate how good an event will make them feel and for how long (the impact bias).

Wilson and Gilbert, Current Directions in Psychological Science, 2005

Most people's happiness baseline is mildly positive, differs between people, and can shift.

Diener, Lucas and Scollon, American Psychologist, 2006

For most people, happiness kept rising with income; it leveled off around $100,000 only for the least happy group.

Killingsworth, Kahneman and Mellers, PNAS, 2023

How satisfied people were in their relationships at 50 predicted their health at 80 better than their cholesterol did.

Waldinger and Schulz, The Good Life, 2023 (Harvard Study of Adult Development)

Commuters predicted talking to a stranger would be the worst way to spend the ride; those asked to do it had the most pleasant commutes.

Epley and Schroeder, Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 2014

After talking with someone new, people underestimate how much the other person liked them (the liking gap).

Boothby et al., Psychological Science, 2018

It takes about 50 hours together to go from acquaintance to casual friend, about 90 to friend, and more than 200 to close friend.

Hall, Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, 2019
